title: Flip a Matrix Over Its Diagonal
statement:
You get a 2D integer array matrix with m rows and n columns. Return its transpose: the matrix mirrored across its main diagonal, so rows become columns.

The result has n rows and m columns, and the value at row i, column j of the result is matrix[j][i]. The matrix need not be square.

examples.why: A 2 × 3 matrix becomes 3 × 2. The first column, 7 and 5, becomes the first row.
A single cell is its own mirror image.
The diagonal 1 and 4 stays put; the 2 and 3 trade places.

hints: What are the dimensions of the result?
Create an n × m result. Each value matrix[i][j] has exactly one place to go.
Loop over every (i, j) of the input and write result[j][i] = matrix[i][j]. Swapping in place only works when the matrix is square.

explain.intuition:
Transposing just swaps the roles of the two indexes: the value at (row i, column j) moves to (row j, column i). Think of rotating a data table so the column headers become row headers.

For a square matrix you could swap pairs in place across the diagonal. For a rectangular one the shape changes, so build a new n × m array and copy each value to its mirrored spot.
steps: Let m = number of rows and n = number of columns.
Create a result with n rows of m columns.
pitfalls: Allocating the result as m × n (the input shape). It breaks for every non-square matrix.
Swapping in place over the whole matrix, which swaps each pair twice and leaves the matrix unchanged.
Filling the result with new Array(n).fill(new Array(m)), which makes every row the same array object.

solutions.title: Copy into a new n × m array
solutions.idea: Allocate the swapped shape and write each value to its mirrored position.

solutions.title: Build each column as a row
solutions.idea: Row j of the result is column j of the input, read top to bottom.

followups: The matrix is square. Transpose it in place with O(1) extra space.
